title: HTTP client stack
issueTitle: HTTP client stack for BotTools: suspend transport, outbound-URL guard, response cache, call budget and test fakes
function: BotTools needs a suspend HTTP stack: a transport, an outbound-URL guard, a response cache, a call budget and test fakes. This tracking issue designs it as a new Kotlin Multiplatform module `webtools-http`, a feeds module `webtools-feeds` on top of it, the shared `build-logic` with the Java 11 floor that folds in #47, and their documentation, and builds it as eleven units, each a sub-issue planned and built on its own board.

wip.detail: Unit 1, #61 (`build-logic`), landed through PR #74 as 1e27071 with no version moved. Unit 2, #47 (`java-floor`), is in progress: its run started at the plan step, its one blocker #61 has landed. Unit 3, #62 (`http-core`), is up next and waits on #47. Units 4 to 11 follow in landing order.

gap.summary: Every published artifact is Java 23 bytecode declaring `org.gradle.jvm.version: 23`, while the README promises JDK 11 or newer. No build file sets `jvmToolchain`, `jvmTarget` or `-Xjdk-release`.
evidence: 47-java-23-bytecode/research/java-11-floor.md F1-F5 — `jvmTarget` alone compiles JDK 21 calls; with `-Xjdk-release=11` they are rejected

options.name: `WebToolsBuild.JAVA_FLOOR = 11` wiring `jvmTarget`, `-Xjdk-release` and the KMP attribute, with a `verifyJavaFloor` guard in `check`
options.why: The API limit on the build JDK without the foojay bump; the guard fails the build rather than let a Java 23 class or a wrong attribute reach a publication.

options.name: `jvmToolchain(11)` as the floor
options.why: The same API limit at the cost of the foojay bump and a JDK 11 on every consumer's composite machine, and it still writes no KMP attribute.
options.wins: If the level tests had to run on a JDK 11 inside this work.

verdict.summary: Add `JAVA_FLOOR = 11` and wire `jvmTarget`, `-Xjdk-release` and the Java compatibility settings (JVM plugin) and the `TargetJvmVersion` attribute (KMP plugin) from it; add `verifyJavaFloor` into `check`; set `1.0.0a` on `webtools-scraping` and `webtools-browser` and extend `webtools-udp`'s `2.0.0a` note; add the build-JDK note to the README.
verdict.defense: A bug fix to bytecode and metadata with no public API, state or wire change, local to the build.
tests: `verifyJavaFloor`: no class above major 55, `org.gradle.jvm.version` 11 on every API and runtime variant
risks: `1.0.0a` orders below `1.0.0`: a consumer graph that also asks for `1.0.0` keeps the defect unless it pins with `strictly`; the README and the release note say so

gap.summary: No HTTP stack exists. `Connector` is the only HTTP client: a blocking, stateful line reader over `URLConnection` that sets the JVM-wide `http.agent` on every connect and calls `Unirest.setTimeouts(0, 0)` in its `init`. Nothing offers a suspend request, a typed failure model or a transport port.

options.name: Open failure hierarchy in `kotlin.Result`, builders over `internal` constructors, one opt-in marker through `@SubclassOptInRequired`
options.why: Adding a failure leaf or a builder property never breaks a consumer's compiled code, and the supplied defaults are usable without opting in.

options.name: A sealed failure root, or enums for library-produced reasons
options.why: Each added leaf or entry is a compile error in a consumer's exhaustive `when` and a runtime `NoWhenBranchMatchedException` in a compiled one.

options.name: Flat constructors with defaulted parameters plus hidden deprecated overloads
options.why: A permanent overload per addition kept correct by hand; `@IntroducedAt` is Kotlin 2.3+.

options.name: `kotlin.time.Clock`/`Instant` or kotlinx-datetime in signatures
options.why: An error-level opt-in on every 2.2.x consumer, and the budget needs no calendar arithmetic.

options.name: `fun interface` for `WallClock`
options.why: A `fun interface` cannot carry the subclass gate; one rule for every seam.

options.name: An opaque `Scheduling` type in place of `CoroutineDispatcher`, keeping coroutines `implementation`
options.why: A consumer could no longer pass its own dispatcher, and the coroutines runtime is part of what a suspend API is.

options.name: kotlin-logging in `commonMain`
options.why: A startup line and a runtime dependency on every consumer, with no gain on one published target; an `internal expect fun` seam is the smallest thing that logs.

options.name: A published `js` target instead of check-only modules
options.why: A coordinate and a klib nothing consumes, Node and Yarn downloads for tests, and a published surface the requirements do not name.
options.wins: The day a non-JVM consumer exists.

options.name: KGP's built-in `abiValidation` instead of BCV
options.why: Experimental on 2.2.0 and its DSL changed by 2.4.

verdict.summary: Create `webtools-http` (KMP plugin, `explicitApi()`, the ABI dump) and `webtools-http-commoncheck` with the `webtools.kotlin-common-check` plugin; deliver the marker, the failure model, the request and response types, `HttpTransport`, `WallClock`, the logging seam and the internal `flatMap`; add the README artifact row and install line.
verdict.defense: One system: one new module's additive API. Its plan starts with the compile proof of the marker, a gated interface, a default naming it and a consumer without opt-in.
tests: Level 4a in `commonTest`: parsing, validation, query encoding
`jvmTest`: the `Url`-vs-`HttpUrl` differential
risks: The public surface has not been compiled; the opt-in behaviour comes from compiler test data and one JVM-only measurement

gap.summary: Nothing decides which URLs may be fetched. OkHttp never consults `Dns` for a digits-and-dots or colon host, so a resolver guard alone misses every IP-literal host, and native redirect follow-up reached `169.254.169.254` through a resolver guard.
evidence: research/http-transport.md — interceptors run after the connect

options.name: A closed `Trusted`/`Untrusted` pair checked in three layers: pre-check, resolver guard, socket factory
options.why: Every layer alone leaks (measured on 39 host forms); together the socket factory backstops the resolver guard.

options.name: A resolver guard only, or a network interceptor or `EventListener` as the guard
options.why: A resolver guard misses every IP-literal host; interceptors run after the connect and a listener cannot veto.

options.name: A consumer-implemented `UrlGuard` seam at 1.0.0
options.why: A callback that can return "allow" can silently defeat `Untrusted`, and no real consumer has shaped the seam.

verdict.summary: Deliver `OutboundUrlPolicy` with `Trusted`/`Untrusted` builders, `TransportSettings` with both default sets, the `internal` classification core in `commonMain`, and the JVM enforcement types with stub-based Level 2 tests.
tests: Level 4a in `commonTest`: every IANA row's first and last address, the host-form catalogue, the published bypass vectors
`jvmTest`: the JDK-predicate-gap and differential tests
risks: Every `TransportSettings` number is a judgement default, not a measurement

gap.summary: OkHttp 5.5.0 re-sends a `503` carrying `Retry-After: 0` and a `421` regardless of client flags, strips only `Authorization` on a cross-host redirect, and a body read after `executeAsync` returns is not cancellable (29.4 s against 0 ms).

options.name: A manual redirect loop, a fail-closed one-exchange guard and a capped body read inside the callback
options.why: One request per hop whatever re-send paths OkHttp has, the hop check before the socket, and cancellation that reaches the body.

options.name: OkHttp-native redirects
options.why: The hop check would run after the socket, only `Authorization` is stripped, the cap is fixed at 20.

options.name: `okhttp-coroutines`' `executeAsync` as published
options.why: It requires coroutines 1.11.0, and the body read after it returns is not cancellable.

options.name: A public `OkHttpClient` in a signature
options.why: No library type in a public signature; the donor client stays an `internal` constructor parameter for the fixtures.

verdict.summary: Deliver `OkHttpTransport` (factory and `internal` constructor), `ExchangeGuard`, the redirect loop, the capped in-callback body read, the failure mapping, `close()` and the transport's logging; add `LoopbackTransports`, `webtoolsUrl`, `toMockResponse` and `enqueue(fixture)` to the fixtures.
verdict.defense: One system: an additive subsystem of `webtools-http`.
tests: Level 3 against `mockwebserver3`: one request for `503` + `Retry-After: 0`, `408`, `429` and each hop; caps; cancel during an endless body; hop 2 refused
Level 4c: slow drip, endless chunked, redirect chain over the cap
risks: A consumer's newer OkHttp 5.x wins resolution; the fail-closed guard does not depend on which re-send paths exist

gap.summary: No response cache exists. Caffeine 3.3.1's `AsyncCache.get` is single-flight, but exceptional completion logs a WARNING per failure and leaves a joinable failed future, and `CompletionStage.await()` cancels the shared future while `asDeferred().await()` does not.

options.name: A `ResponseCache` port with `CaffeineResponseCache`: failure as a value, `asDeferred` waiting, compare-and-remove for `maxAge`
options.why: One load serves many concurrent callers, a failure is never cached, and one waiter's cancellation does not cancel the shared load.

options.name: A typed cache per endpoint; Aedile; `scope.future { }` with exceptional completion; invalidate-before-get for `maxAge`
options.why: Multiplies bounds; pins Caffeine 3.2.4 and runs loads in the first caller's context; logs a WARNING per failure; ran 10-12 loads for 50 stale callers against 1.

options.name: Cancelling the shared load when the last waiter leaves (Store5)
options.why: A ref-counted multicaster with its own race class; the wasted work is bounded by `maxWait` plus the call timeout.

verdict.summary: Deliver the `ResponseCache` port, `CacheKey`, `CachePolicy`, `Lookup`, `CacheStats`, `ResponseCache.Disabled` and `CaffeineResponseCache` with the load-start, failure-as-value, `asDeferred` waiting, `maxAge` and `Closed` behaviours.
verdict.defense: One system: an additive subsystem of `webtools-http`.
tests: Level 2 on `VirtualClock`: hits, expiry, miss TTL, `maxAge`, coalescing, one waiter's cancellation, close
Level 4a: key canonicalisation
Level 4c: the size bound and the 2,000-retry failure-identity check
risks: A shared load carries the first caller's lane and wait cap

gap.summary: No call budget exists. OpenDota and Open-Meteo count in fixed wall-clock windows and count refused requests; a greedy token bucket let 119 calls into one server minute against 60.

options.name: `WindowedCallBudget`: clock-aligned fixed windows with lanes, pauses on server signals and a hard daily stop
options.why: Aligned windows with a 1 s guard overspent in 0 of 1,000 skewed trials.

options.name: A token bucket, GCRA or Bucket4j as the default
options.why: A greedy bucket doubles at every provider boundary; GCRA paces below what a clock-reset provider allows; Bucket4j is JVM-only, needs Java 17 and offers no suspending FIFO with refunds, lanes or pauses.
options.wins: Later, as another implementation of the port for multi-process counting.

options.name: Lending unused lane reserve
options.why: In a plan-ahead ledger it drove interactive grants to zero (measured).

options.name: Logging through `BudgetObserver` only
options.why: Silent unless every constructing path installs an observer.

verdict.summary: Deliver `CallBudget`, `Permit`, `withPermit`, `Lane`, `RateWindow`, `RateSignals` and their reader, `RetryAfter`, `BudgetStore` with `InMemoryBudgetStore`, `BudgetObserver`, `CallBudget.Unlimited` and `WindowedCallBudget` in `commonMain`, with the non-suspend `close()` plus `flush()`; add `RecordingBudgetObserver` and `FakeBudgetStore` to the fixtures.
verdict.defense: One system: an additive subsystem of `webtools-http`.
tests: Level 2 on `VirtualClock`: FIFO, refunds, lane floors, pauses, hard stop, restore, write-ahead after a crash
Level 4a: the HTTP-date table against `java.time`, window arithmetic, a seeded property test
leaves: Reading signals from a real response (unit 9)
risks: How a `Mutex`-based ledger closes without suspending is unit 8's plan to settle (architecture §13)

gap.summary: The cache, the budget and the transport do not compose themselves, and the order they run in decides what a refusal, a throttle or a decode failure costs a caller.
evidence: architecture.md §7.2 — cache, then budget inside the loader, then transport

options.name: Two facades: `UpstreamClient` for endpoints and `UrlFetcher` for administrator-supplied URLs
options.why: Two types encode the invariant that an untrusted URL cannot reach `call` and `fetch` cannot be handed an endpoint's cache.

options.name: One facade class
options.why: Loses that invariant.

options.name: A decoder per call
options.why: The cache key cannot see it, so inconsistent decoders would corrupt a shared entry.

verdict.summary: Deliver `Endpoint`, `CallSpec`, `FetchSpec`, `UpstreamClient`, `UrlFetcher`, their configs, the common factories and the JVM owning factories with the `maxBurst` dispatcher sizing and the cache → budget → transport closing order; the README how-to.
verdict.defense: One system: an additive subsystem of `webtools-http`.
tests: Level 2 on the fake transport: a refusal costs nothing; a `429` with `Retry-After` pauses the budget; a decode failure is never stored; non-`GET` bypasses the cache
Level 3: a real end-to-end call over loopback
risks: The generic `Endpoint<T>` factory-over-class resolution is argued from precedents and checked in this unit's plan

gap.summary: No feed parsing or conditional GET exists. Rome 2.1.0 refuses DOCTYPE by default but skips a hardening feature its SAX provider does not recognise and last released on 2023-03-12; rssreader 3.12.0 swallows malformed XML into an empty stream and ignores Atom `rel`.

options.name: A multiplatform parser port with a hardened Rome default, a prolog scan, and a stateless conditional GET over `UrlFetcher`
options.why: The port, the scan and a fixed-heap Level 4c suite bound Rome's exposure, and a streaming parser can replace it behind the same port.

options.name: A stateful feed fetcher holding validators
options.why: An unbounded map keyed by administrator-supplied URLs, lost on restart.

options.name: The feed fetcher on `HttpTransport` directly
options.why: `UrlFetcher` gives the free policy pre-check and a throttle as `RateLimited` without parsing `Retry-After` itself.

options.name: rssreader 3.12.0 or prof18's parser as the default
options.why: Silent on malformed XML and ignoring Atom `rel`; or needing Kotlin 2.4.10 and an unhardened SAX parser.

options.name: A JVM-only feeds module
options.why: Ruled out by requirement 4.

options.name: Publishing `FeedParserContract` as a fixtures variant at 1.0.0
options.why: Doubles the exposure to the experimental publishing API, is unprobed for a module whose tests use another module's fixtures, and no second parser exists to use it.

verdict.summary: Create `webtools-feeds` and its check module; deliver the port, model, limits, validators, `FeedFetch`, `FeedFailure`, `FeedFetcher` and the prolog scan in `commonMain`, `RomeFeedParser` and `FeedFetcher.untrusted` in `jvmMain`; README artifact row, install line and how-to.
verdict.defense: One new module built on published seams; depending on a sibling module does not make it two systems.
tests: Level 2 on the fakes: conditional headers, `304` → `NotModified`
Level 3 through `LoopbackTransports.untrusted`
Level 4a: the prolog scan and the id and link rules
Level 4c: the hardening suite with a fixed heap
risks: Rome is dormant and its DOM amplification on a hostile 2 MiB document is unmeasured

impact.summary: Two new Kotlin Multiplatform artifacts, `webtools-http` and `webtools-feeds` 1.0.0, add a suspend HTTP stack and a feed parser for BotTools, with a published test-fixtures variant. The three existing artifacts change only by the Java 11 floor, and no existing source or public API changes. The tracking plan moves no version itself; each unit's release is its own.

release.note: `java-floor` is the only unit that moves an existing artifact's version; the two new modules stay unreleased at 1.0.0 until the last unit lands

downstream.summary: They see only the Java 11 floor: Java 11 bytecode declaring `org.gradle.jvm.version: 11`, loadable on JDK 11 to 22. POMs and public API are unchanged.

The HTTP stack: transport, URL policies, cache, budget, facades and failure model, with `kotlinx-coroutines-core` as `api` and `okhttp-jvm`, `caffeine` and `slf4j-api` at runtime only; a test-fixtures variant carries the fakes.
An RSS/Atom parser port with the Rome default and a conditional-GET fetcher, built on `webtools-http`.

The first consumer, through an internal adapter. Its release conditions (Java 21 or lower bytecode, Kotlin 2.2.x-readable metadata, no `-SNAPSHOT` dependency) hold for both new artifacts; its adapter building against the Experimental seams lets them graduate.
`./gradlew build` adds `verifyJavaFloor`, `apiCheck` on the new modules, the fixtures-publication check and the check-only JS compiles; `build-logic` brings its own level tests, run on demand.

adaptation.summary: Move to the lettered versions of the existing artifacts once published, requesting them `strictly` where the graph also asks for the plain release.
Implementing or subclassing a gated seam needs `@OptIn(ExperimentalForInheritanceWebToolsApi::class)`; calling and passing it do not.
Unchanged; moving `Connector`'s fetches onto `webtools-http` is a follow-up after its release.

api.surface: `webtools-http` and `webtools-feeds` value types, configs and supplied defaults
api.summary: Final classes built by factory and builder; no public `data class` and no defaulted parameters on Stable Core functions.
Interfaces with supplied defaults; implementing one needs the opt-in, and each graduates to `@SupportedExtension` once BotTools' adapter has built against it.
Stable Core with source compatibility only: no ABI dump covers the fixtures jar.
Internal to the repository and not published.

units.summary: No downstream effect: the three artifacts' POMs, module metadata and jars are identical to `834ce4a`'s, so no version moved. Inside the repository, `build-logic` holds the shared configuration the later units build on.

Every module compiles to Java 11 bytecode against the Java 11 API and declares `org.gradle.jvm.version: 11`, so consumers on JDK 11 to 22 can load the lettered versions once published. No source or public API change.
